o: Shift an unsigned eight-bit binary number left or right.
Explain the relationship between shifts and powers of two.
r: What does hexadecimal F represent in denary?
What happens if a binary addition exceeds 255?
Overflow; an eighth bit cannot hold the full result.
c: A shift moves bit positions
Move every bit the same number of columns. Keep the length at eight bits.
Left shift
Move bits left, add zeros at the right. Multiply by 2 per place if no 1 is lost.
Right shift
Move bits right, add zeros at the left. Divide the unsigned value by 2 per place, discarding remainders.
Bits can be lost
The result is only the eight bits that remain. A bit pushed beyond an edge is discarded.

m.q: Shift 00010110 left by 2 places. Explain each step.
st: Label the eight bit positions 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1.
Start with 00010110, which is 16 + 4 + 2 = 22.
Move every bit two positions to the left; fill two positions on the right with zeros.
The eight-bit result is 01011000, which is 88.
Check: 22 × 2² = 88. This time no 1 was lost.

w: Shift 00101000 right by one place.
00010100, representing 20 rather than 40.
Shift 00001101 left by two places.
00110100, representing 52.
Why does 11000000 shifted left by two places not show 768?
The two leading 1s leave the eight-bit register, so the result is 00000000.

k.q: Predict the displayed answer and complete a one-line change on your MWB.
p: Predict the output of this program.
Change the arithmetic to model a two-place left shift.
Explain when multiplying by a power of two is NOT the same as an 8-bit shift.
k.a: 24; for two places write print(value * 4), giving 48. If bits are discarded by the eight-bit limit the arithmetic model can differ. On this lesson, pupils begin on MWBs; the teacher may then introduce running code in the OCR ERL editor.

e: Perform an 8-bit logical right shift of 10110000 by three places. [2]
00010110. All bits move three places right and zeroes fill from the left.
Explain the effect of a one-place left binary shift, giving one limitation. [3]
Each bit moves left one position; a zero enters at the right; the unsigned number usually doubles, but a leading 1 can be discarded.
A pupil claims shifting 10000000 left once gives 256 in an 8-bit register. Explain the mistake. [2]
The 1 is shifted out and lost; the eight-bit result is 00000000, not 256.
v: Moving each bit left or right, filling empty positions with zero.
The leftmost bit with the highest place value.
The rightmost bit with the smallest place value.
A result that cannot fit into the available number of bits.
x: A one-place logical right shift always adds a zero on the left.

o: Explain why computers store characters as binary codes.
Describe a character set and distinguish ASCII from Unicode.
Work out character-set capacity from a bit count.
r: What does a one-place left binary shift normally do to an unsigned value?
Doubles it if no significant bits are lost.
Challenge: how many different patterns can five bits represent?
c: A character set
Every supported character is assigned a distinct numerical code. Computers store the code as binary.
ASCII
A familiar character set. Standard ASCII uses 7 bits for 128 possible codes; an 8-bit extension can have more.
Unicode
A much larger standard covering writing systems, symbols and emojis. The number of bytes depends on its encoding.
More bits, more possible codes
n bits can represent 2ⁿ different codes. Different character sets are needed because 128 codes are not enough for every language.

m.q: Explain how a keyboard letter becomes binary.
st: Choose the character 'A'.
Look up its numerical code in standard ASCII: 65.
Convert 65 to binary: 64 + 1 = 01000001 in eight bits.
Store and transmit the bits. The text is displayed again by looking up the code.
Explain: 'a' is a different character and has a different code (97).

w: Write the eight-bit binary form of ASCII code 66.
A character set has 6 bits per character. How many codes?
Why might Unicode be preferable for a multilingual school?
It can represent many more scripts and special symbols than standard ASCII.

k.q: Complete the character-code program on your mini-whiteboard.
p: Write one instruction to display the word 'Hello' rather than its numerical code.
k.a: Initially displays 65; change to characterCode = 66; a valid third line is print("Hello"). The numeric code is not automatically converted to its character by print().

e: Define a character set. [2]
A collection of supported characters with a unique binary code assigned to each one.
Standard ASCII uses seven bits. Calculate how many distinct codes are possible. [2]
Give two reasons why Unicode is useful for a global messaging application. [2]
Supports more languages/scripts and a wider range of symbols/emojis.
v: A mapping between characters and binary codes.
A character encoding with a standard seven-bit code set.
A standard representing characters from many writing systems.
A system for turning characters into stored binary codes.
x: The letter A and the lower-case letter a have the same ASCII code.

o: Describe a bitmap as a grid of pixels.
Explain resolution, colour depth and metadata.
Predict the effects of changing image settings.
r: A mapping of characters to unique codes.
How many binary patterns can four bits represent?
Challenge: what is the eight-bit value of 01011010?
c: Bitmap images
A picture is stored as a grid of pixels. Each pixel has a binary-coded colour.
Resolution
Width × height in pixels. More pixels normally produce more detail and larger uncompressed files.
Colour depth
The number of bits used for each pixel. Four bits allow 16 possible colour codes.
Metadata
Information about the image such as width, height and colour depth, stored alongside pixel data.

m.q: Work out the colour possibilities of a small bitmap.
st: Draw a 4 × 3 grid. It contains 12 pixels.
Suppose each pixel uses 2 bits.
List possible binary codes: 00, 01, 10 and 11.
Therefore each pixel can be one of four coded colours.
Total raw pixel data: 12 × 2 = 24 bits (metadata excluded).

w: How many pixels are in a 6 × 4 bitmap?
6 × 4 = 24 pixels.
How many colours are available with 3-bit colour depth?
2³ = 8 possible colours.
Explain why 8-bit colour depth uses more storage than 4-bit at the same resolution.
Each pixel requires twice as many bits (8 rather than 4).

k.q: Predict and modify a simple raw-image calculation.
p: Predict the number of pixels displayed.
Write one new expression to find bits when each pixel takes 2 bits.
k.a: 12 pixels; changing width to 6 gives 18; print(width * height * 2) gives the pixel data in bits (36 with the revised width).

e: A bitmap is 10 pixels wide and 8 high. Calculate the pixel count. [2]
10 × 8 = 80 pixels.
State what colour depth measures, then calculate the maximum colours at 5 bits per pixel. [3]
Bits used for each pixel; 2⁵ = 32 colours.
Explain the difference between resolution and metadata. [3]
Resolution is width × height in pixels; metadata describes image properties such as resolution or colour depth.
v: Smallest individual coloured element in a bitmap.
Width and height measured in pixels.
Number of bits used for each pixel.
Data about the image, such as dimensions and colour depth.
x: A bitmap with higher colour depth can represent more colours per pixel.

o: Calculate an uncompressed bitmap’s raw pixel-data size.
Convert image sizes from bits to bytes.
Explain the impact of resolution and colour depth.
r: How many pixels are in a 5 × 6 bitmap?
Convert the binary number 00010000 into denary.
Challenge: what happens to raw image size if width doubles but other settings stay the same?
c: Raw image formula
Width (pixels) × height (pixels) × colour depth (bits/pixel) = total bits.
Bits to bytes
Divide bits by 8. OCR J277 questions may ask for bytes or larger units.
State assumptions
This formula estimates raw pixel data. File headers, metadata and compression can change actual file size.
Work methodically
Write the formula, substitute numbers, calculate bits and then convert units. Always write units.

m.q: Calculate the raw size of a 200 × 100 image at 8-bit colour.
st: Identify width = 200 and height = 100 pixels.
Multiply by colour depth: 20,000 × 8 = 160,000 bits.
Divide by 8: 160,000 ÷ 8 = 20,000 bytes.
For decimal units, 20,000 bytes = 20 KB (ignoring headers).

w: Find bits for a 40 × 20 image at 4 bits per pixel.
Convert 3,200 bits to bytes.
An image’s colour depth rises from 4 to 8. How does raw size change?
It doubles at the same width and height.

k.q: Write the calculation as code before using the editor.
k.code:
width = 20
height = 10
depth = 8
print(width * height * depth)
p: Predict the number of bits displayed.
Change depth to 4 and predict again.
Add a second print instruction to display bytes.
k.a: 1,600 bits; with depth 4: 800 bits; print(width * height * depth DIV 8) gives 100 bytes at depth 4.

e: Calculate the raw pixel-data size of a 100 × 80 image at 2-bit colour depth. Give bits. [3]
Convert the result into bytes. [2]
Explain why the actual saved file may differ from the raw result. [2]
File metadata/headers and compression may change the size.
v: Storage required to represent the image.
Stored without reducing the original pixel data.
x: To convert an image file size from bits into bytes, multiply by eight.

o: Explain how analogue sound is represented digitally.
Distinguish sample rate from bit depth.
Explain effects on quality and uncompressed file size.
r: Data describing a file, such as image dimensions.
Challenge: a 10 × 10 bitmap uses 2 bits per pixel. How many bits?
c: Analogue sound is continuous
Sound travels as a wave. The microphone’s changing electrical signal represents amplitude.
Sampling
The analogue signal’s amplitude is measured at regular time intervals.
Sample rate
Number of samples taken per second, measured in hertz (Hz). Higher sample rate usually captures more detail.
Bit depth
Bits used to store each sampled amplitude. Greater bit depth allows more distinct amplitude levels.
File size
Uncompressed mono sound: sample rate × duration × bit depth (in bits); compressed formats differ.

m.q: Sketch how a continuous sound becomes digital samples.
st: Draw a smooth analogue wave on a time axis.
Place five equally spaced vertical sample positions.
At each position, mark the wave’s amplitude.
Turn each measured amplitude into a binary value.
Explain how more frequent samples and greater bit depth can improve fidelity while increasing file size.

w: At 1,000 Hz, how many samples are taken each second?
1,000 samples.
At 4,000 samples/s for 3 s, how many samples?
12,000 samples.
Explain the difference between sample rate and bit depth.
Sample rate is measurements per second; bit depth is bits stored per measurement.

k.q: Start by modelling a sample count in OCR ERL.
p: Extend with a bitDepth variable of 8 and print the number of bits.
k.a: 6,000 samples initially; 10,000 samples at 5 s; bitDepth = 8 and print(rate * seconds * bitDepth) gives 80,000 bits for the revised duration.

e: Describe sound sampling. [2]
Measure the amplitude of an analogue signal at regular intervals and represent each sample digitally.
State the unit of sample rate. [1]
Hertz (Hz), samples per second.
Explain two effects of increasing bit depth. [4]
More amplitude levels / potentially more accurate reproduction; each sample needs more bits, increasing uncompressed file size.
v: Measuring an analogue signal’s amplitude at intervals.
Number of amplitude measurements per second.
Bits used to represent each sound sample.
x: Bit depth means how many samples are taken each second.
